entries.7b4f45056ba5574573aa80b13b1175e06bc293f3: <div sID="gen14019" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="17" osisID="Prov.17" sID="Prov.17"/> <div eID="gen14019" type="x-p"/>
entries.04712c37c3269fe9b37a1bc2d533602465e0acbd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv44"/><title type="x-s3">Falsehood and Oppression Reproved.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv44"/> <div sID="gen14020" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Better <hi type="italic">is</hi> a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices <hi type="italic">with</hi> strife. <div eID="gen14020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14021" type="x-p"/> These words recommend family-love and peace, as conducing very much to the comfort of human life. 1. Those that live in unity and quietness, not only free from jealousies and animosities, but vying in mutual endearments, and obliging to one another, live very comfortably, though they are low in the world, work hard and fare hard, though they have but each of them <hi type="italic">a morsel,</hi> and that <hi type="italic">a dry morsel.</hi> There may be peace and quietness where there are not three meals a day, provided there by a joint satisfaction in God's providence and a mutual satisfaction in each other's prudence. Holy love may be found in a cottage. 2. Those that live in contention, that are always jarring and brawling, and reflecting upon one another, though they have plenty of dainties, <hi type="italic">a house full of sacrifices,</hi> live uncomfortably; they cannot expect the blessing of God upon them and what they have, nor can they have any true relish of their enjoyments, much less any peace in their own consciences. Love will sweeten a <hi type="italic">dry morsel,</hi> but strife will sour and embitter <hi type="italic">a house full of sacrifices.</hi> A little of the leaven of malice will leaven all the enjoyments.
entries.f64d6958d3ccd6103d2f5e6a22432313d1c3c97c: <div eID="gen14021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14022" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">2</hi> A wise servant shall have rule over a son that causeth shame, and shall have part of the inheritance among the brethren. <div eID="gen14022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14023" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. True merit does not go by dignity. All agree that the son in the family is more worthy than the servant (<reference osisRef="John.8.35">John viii. 35</reference>), and yet sometimes it so happens that the servant is wise, and a blessing and credit to the family, when the son is a fool, and a burden and shame to the family. Eliezer of Damascus, though Abram could not bear to think that he should be his heir, was a stay to the family, when he obtained a wife for Isaac; whereas Ishmael, a son, was a shame to it, when he mocked Isaac. 2. True dignity will go by merit. If a servant be wise, and manage things well, he shall be further trusted, and not only <hi type="italic">have rule</hi> with, but <hi type="italic">rule over a son that causes shame;</hi> for God and nature have designed that <hi type="italic">the fool shall be servant to the wise in heart.</hi> Nay, a prudent servant may perhaps come to have such an interest in his master as to be taken in for a child's share of the estate and to <hi type="italic">have part of the inheritance among the brethren.</hi>
entries.5aca52104204987c99b22fecc7556e273f53f03b: <div eID="gen14023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14024" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> The fining pot <hi type="italic">is</hi> for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> trieth the hearts. <div eID="gen14024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14025" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The hearts of the children of men are subject, not only to God's view, but to his judgment: As <hi type="italic">the fining-pot is for silver,</hi> both to prove it and to improve it so <hi type="italic">the Lord tries the hearts;</hi> he searches whether they are standard or no, and those that are he refines and makes purer, <reference osisRef="Jer.17.10">Jer. xvii. 10</reference>. God tries the heart by affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.10-Ps.66.11">Ps. lxvi. 10, 11</reference>), and often chooses his people in that furnace (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Isa. xlviii. 10</reference>) and makes them choice. 2. It is God only that <hi type="italic">tries the hearts.</hi> Men may try their <hi type="italic">silver</hi> and <hi type="italic">gold</hi> with <hi type="italic">the fining-pot and the furnace,</hi> but they have no such way of trying one another's hearts; God only does that, who is both the searcher and the sovereign of the heart.
entries.619326d1e9a010555fafb188298de8ea4e1f5080: <div eID="gen14025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14026" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> A wicked doer giveth heed to false lips; <hi type="italic">and</hi> a liar giveth ear to a naughty tongue. <div eID="gen14026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14027" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that design to do ill support themselves by falsehood and lying: <hi type="italic">A wicked doer gives</hi> ear, with a great deal of pleasure, <hi type="italic">to false lips,</hi> that will justify him in the ill he does, to those that aim to make public disturbances, catch greedily at libels, and false stories, that defame the government and the administration. 2. Those that take the liberty to tell lies take a pleasure in hearing them told: <hi type="italic">A liar gives</hi> heed to a malicious backbiting tongue, that he may have something to graft his lies upon, and with which to give them some colour of truth and so to support them. Sinners will strengthen one another's hands; and those show that they are bad themselves who court the acquaintance and need the assistance of those that are bad.
entries.68308b7aba026f2fb07d84ecec83854ce835238a: <div eID="gen14027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14028" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Whoso mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that is glad at calamities shall not be unpunished. <div eID="gen14028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14029" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What a great sin those are guilty of who trample upon the poor, who ridicule their wants and the meanness of their appearance, upbraid them with their poverty, and take advantage from their weakness to be abusive and injurious to them. They <hi type="italic">reproach their Maker,</hi> put a great contempt and affront upon him, who allotted the poor to the condition they are in, owns them, and takes care of them, and can, when he pleases, reduce us to that condition. Let those that thus reproach their Maker know that they shall be called to an account for it, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.40-Matt.25.41">Matt. xxv. 40, 41</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.14.31">Prov. xiv. 31</reference>. 2. What great danger those are in of falling into trouble themselves who are pleased to see and hear of the troubles of others: <hi type="italic">He that is glad at calamities,</hi> that he may be built up upon the ruins of others, and regales himself with the judgments of God when they are abroad, let him know that he <hi type="italic">shall not go unpunished;</hi> the cup shall be put into his hand, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.6-Ezek.25.7">Ezek. xxv. 6, 7</reference>.  <div eID="gen14029" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c722cb75ce9b6adbb549c7a45607b0f7dfa6bd4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv45"/><title type="x-s3">Common Truths.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv45"/> <div sID="gen14030" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Children's children <hi type="italic">are</hi> the crown of old men; and the glory of children <hi type="italic">are</hi> their fathers. <div eID="gen14030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14031" type="x-p"/> They are so, that is, they should be so, and, if they conduct themselves worthily, they are so. 1. It is an honour to parents when they are old to leave children, and <hi type="italic">children's children,</hi> growing up, that tread in the steps of their virtues, and are likely to maintain and advance the reputation of their families. It is an honour to a man to live so long as to see his children's children (<reference osisRef="Ps.128.6">Ps. cxxviii. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.50.23">Gen. l. 23</reference>), to see his house built up in them, and to see them likely to serve their generation according to the will of God. This crowns and completes their comfort in this world. 2. It is an honour to children to have wise and godly parents, and to have them continued to them even after they have themselves grown up and settled in the world. Those are unnatural children who reckon their aged parents a burden to them, and think they live too long; whereas, if the children be wise and good, it is as much their honour as can be that thereby they are comforts to their parents in the unpleasant days of their old age.
entries.3aa46f965c82ed1768eb99258f2ef1e8216b2bfc: <div eID="gen14031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14032" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">7</hi> Excellent speech becometh not a fool: much less do lying lips a prince. <div eID="gen14032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14033" type="x-p"/> Two things are here represented as very absurd: 1. That men of no repute should be dictators. What can be more unbecoming than for fools, who are known to have little sense and discretion, to pretend to that which is above them and which they were never cut out for? A fool, in Solomon's proverbs, signifies a wicked man, whom <hi type="italic">excellent speech</hi> does not become, because his conversation gives the lie to his excellent speech. What have those to do to declare God's statutes who <hi type="italic">hate instruction?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.16">Ps. l. 16</reference>. Christ would not suffer the unclean spirits to say that they knew him to be the Son of God. See <reference osisRef="Acts.16.17-Acts.16.18">Acts xvi. 17, 18</reference>. 2. That men of great repute should be deceivers. If it is unbecoming a despicable man to presume to speak as a philosopher or politician, and nobody heeds him, being prejudiced against his character, much more unbecoming is it for a prince, for a man of honour, to take advantage from his character and the confidence that is put in him to lie, and dissemble, and make no conscience of breaking his word. Lying ill becomes any man, but worst a prince, so corrupt is the modern policy, which insinuates that princes ought not to make themselves slaves to their words further than is for their interest, and <hi type="italic">Qui nescit dissimulare nescit regnare—He who knows not how to dissemble knows not how to reign.</hi>
entries.e1cc9bd3231e445ca86c52c40af2715c6a7845d5: <div eID="gen14033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14034" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> A gift <hi type="italic">is as</hi> a precious stone in the eyes of him that hath it: whithersoever it turneth, it prospereth. <div eID="gen14034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14035" type="x-p"/> The design of this observation is to show, 1. That those who have money in their hand think they can do any thing with it. Rich men value a little money as if it were a <hi type="italic">precious stone,</hi> and value themselves on it as if it gave them not only ornament, but power, and every one were bound to be at their beck, even justice itself. Whithersoever they turn this sparkling diamond they expect it should dazzle the eyes of all, and make them do just what they would have them do in hopes of it. The deepest bag will carry the cause. Fee high, and you may have what you will. 2. That those who have money in their eye, and set their hearts upon it, will do any thing for it: <hi type="italic">A bribe is as a precious stone in the eyes of him that takes it;</hi> it has a great influence upon him, and he will be sure to go the way that it leads him, hither and thither, though contrary to justice and not consistent with himself.
entries.aa94ca93e0ed3d3079f5065a1f7ef9b3ea82cbc7: <div eID="gen14035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14036" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">9</hi> He that covereth a transgression seeketh love; but he that repeateth a matter separateth <hi type="italic">very</hi> friends. <div eID="gen14036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14037" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. The way to preserve peace among relations and neighbours is to make the best of every thing, not to tell others what has been said or done against them when it is not at all necessary to their safety, nor to take notice of what has been said or done against them when it is not at all necessary to their safety, nor to take notice of what has been said or done against ourselves, but to excuse both, and put the best construction upon them. "It was an oversight; therefore overlook it. It was done through forgetfulness; therefore forget it. It perhaps made nothing of you; do you make nothing of it." 2. The ripping up of faults is the ripping out of love, and nothing tends more to the separating of friends, and setting them at variance, than the <hi type="italic">repeating of matters</hi> that have been in variance; for they commonly lose nothing in the repetition, but the things themselves are aggravated and the passions about them revived and exasperated. The best method of peace is by an amnesty or act of oblivion.
entries.9e151529216c0e0970898037596af34e24e5dbf4: <div eID="gen14037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14038" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> A reproof entereth more into a wise man than an hundred stripes into a fool. <div eID="gen14038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14039" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A word is enough to the wise. A gentle reproof will enter not only into the head, but into the heart of a wise man, so as to have a strong influence upon him; for, if but a hint be given to conscience, let it alone to carry it on and prosecute it. 2. Stripes are not enough for a fool, to make him sensible of his errors, that he may repent of them, and be more cautious for the future. He that is sottish and wilful is very rarely benefited by severity. David is softened with, <hi type="italic">Thou art the man;</hi> but Pharaoh remains hard under all the plagues of Egypt.
entries.e021e0748b12f81cd419bf89fceff663a5a22f31: <div eID="gen14039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14040" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> An evil <hi type="italic">man</hi> seeketh only rebellion: therefore a cruel messenger shall be sent against him. <div eID="gen14040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14041" type="x-p"/> Here is the sin and punishment of an evil man. 1. His sin. He is an evil man indeed that seeks all occasions to rebel against God, and the government God has set over him, and to contradict and quarrel with those about him. <hi type="italic">Quærit jurgia—He picks quarrels;</hi> so some. There are some that are actuated by a spirit of opposition, that will contradict for contradiction-sake, that will go on frowardly in their wicked ways in spite of all restraint and check. <hi type="italic">A rebellious man seeks mischief</hi> (so some read it), watches all opportunities to disturb the public peace. 2. His punishment. Because he will not be reclaimed by mild and gentle methods, <hi type="italic">a cruel messenger shall be sent against him,</hi> some dreadful judgment or other, as a messenger from God. Angels, God's messengers, shall be employed as ministers of his justice against him, <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Ps. lxxviii. 49</reference>. Satan, the angel of death, shall be let loose upon him, and the <hi type="italic">messengers</hi> of Satan. His prince shall send a sergeant to arrest him, an executioner to cut him off. He that <hi type="italic">kicks against the pricks</hi> is <hi type="italic">waited for of the sword.</hi>  <div eID="gen14041" type="x-p"/>
entries.034a9a8f8d2549b4e3745623e0db25314d480387: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv46"/><title type="x-s3">Weighty Sayings.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv46"/> <div sID="gen14042" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">12</hi> Let a bear robbed of her whelps meet a man, rather than a fool in his folly. <div eID="gen14042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14043" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. A passionate man is a brutish man. However at other times he may have some wisdom, take him in his passion ungoverned, and he is a <hi type="italic">fool in his folly;</hi> those are fools in whose bosom anger rests and in whose countenance anger rages. He has put off man, and is become like a bear, a raging bear, <hi type="italic">a bear robbed of her whelps;</hi> he is as fond of the gratifications of his lusts and passions as a bear of her whelps (which, though ugly, are her own), as eager in the pursuit of them as she is in quest of her whelps when they are missing, and as full of indignation if crossed in the pursuit. 2. He is a dangerous man, falls foul of every one that stands in his way, though innocent, though his friend, as a bear robbed of her whelps sets upon the first man she meets as the robber. <hi type="italic">Ira furor brevis est—Anger is temporary madness.</hi> One may more easily stop, escape, or guard against an enraged bear, than an outrageous angry man. Let us therefore watch over our own passions (lest they get head and do mischief) and so consult our own honour; and let us avoid the company of furious men, and get out of their way when they are in their fury, and so consult our own safety. <hi type="italic">Currenti cede furori—Give place unto wrath.</hi>
entries.12191b93eb1685f509c0601125b64659bff9286e: <div eID="gen14043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14044" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Whoso rewardeth evil for good, evil shall not depart from his house. <div eID="gen14044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14045" type="x-p"/> A malicious mischievous man is here represented, 1. As ungrateful to his friends. He oftentimes is so absurd and insensible of kindnesses done him that he renders <hi type="italic">evil for good.</hi> David met with those that were his adversaries for his love, <reference osisRef="Ps.109.4">Ps. cix. 4</reference>. To render evil for evil is brutish, but to render evil for good is devilish. He is an ill-natured man who, because he is resolved not to return a kindness, will revenge it. 2. As therein unkind to his family, for he entails a curse upon it. This is a crime so heinous that it shall be punished, not only in his person, but in his posterity, for whom he thus treasures up wrath. <hi type="italic">The sword shall not depart from</hi> David's <hi type="italic">house</hi> because he rewarded Uriah with evil for his good services. The Jews stoned Christ for his good works; therefore is his blood upon them and upon their children.
entries.9c85604cb82636d3249ef2a88bc4fb84178eeeac: <div eID="gen14045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14046" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> The beginning of strife <hi type="italic">is as</hi> when one letteth out water: therefore leave off contention, before it be meddled with. <div eID="gen14046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14047" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The danger that there is in <hi type="italic">the beginning of strife.</hi> One hot word, one peevish reflection, one angry demand, one spiteful contradiction, begets another, and that a third, and so on, till it proves like the cutting of a dam; when the water has got a little passage it does itself widen the breach, bears down all before it, and there is then no stopping it, no reducing it. 2. A good caution inferred thence, to take heed of the first spark of contention and to put it out as soon as ever it appears. Dread the breaking of the ice, for, if once broken, it will break further; <hi type="italic">therefore leave it off,</hi> not only when you see the worst of it, for then it may be too late, but when you see the first of it. <hi type="italic">Obsta principiis—Resist its earliest display.</hi> Leave it off even <hi type="italic">before it be meddled with;</hi> leave it off, if it were possible, before you begin.
entries.25c1bb91d112c53028517c3c7752f2a10c62ca11: <div eID="gen14047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14048" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both <hi type="italic">are</hi> abomination to the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen14048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14049" type="x-p"/> This shows what an offence it is to God, 1. When those that are entrusted with the administration of public justice, judges, juries, witnesses, prosecutors, counsel, do either acquit the guilty or condemn those that are not guilty, or in the least contribute to either; this defeats the end of government, which is to protect the good and punish the bad, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.3-Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 3, 4</reference>. It is equally provoking to God to <hi type="italic">justify the wicked,</hi> though it be in pity and <hi type="italic">in favorem vitæ—to safe life,</hi> as to <hi type="italic">condemn the just.</hi> 2. When any private persons plead for sin and sinners, palliate and excuse wickedness, or argue against virtue and piety, and so <hi type="italic">pervert the right ways of the Lord</hi> and confound the eternal distinctions between good and evil.
entries.fc6f994122fd1452ded28afd2b9b540d3d8128bf: <div eID="gen14049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14050" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">16</hi> Wherefore <hi type="italic">is there</hi> a price in the hand of a fool to get wisdom, seeing <hi type="italic">he hath</hi> no heart <hi type="italic">to it?</hi> <div eID="gen14050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14051" type="x-p"/> Two things are here spoken of with astonishment:—1. God's great goodness to foolish man, in putting <hi type="italic">a price into his hand to get wisdom,</hi> to get knowledge and grace to fit him for both worlds. We have rational souls, the means of grace, the strivings of the Spirit, access to God by prayer; we have time and opportunity. He that has a good estate (so some understand it) has advantages thereby of getting wisdom by purchasing instruction. Good parents, relations, ministers, friends, are helps to get wisdom. It is <hi type="italic">a price,</hi> therefore of value, a talent. It is <hi type="italic">a price in the hand,</hi> in possession; <hi type="italic">the word is nigh thee.</hi> It is a price for getting; it is for our own advantage; it is for getting wisdom, the very thing which, being fools, we have most need of. We have reason to wonder that God should so consider our necessity, and should entrust us with such advantages, though he foresaw we should not make a right improvement of them. 2. Man's great wickedness, his neglect of God's favour and his own interest, which is very absurd and unaccountable: <hi type="italic">He has no heart to it,</hi> not to the wisdom that is to be got, nor to the price in the use of which it may be got. <hi type="italic">He has no heart,</hi> no skill, nor will, nor courage, to improve his advantages. He has set his heart upon other things, so that he has no heart to his duty or the great concerns of his soul. Wherefore should a price be thrown away and lost upon one so undeserving of it?  <div eID="gen14051" type="x-p"/>
entries.94369cc32f75cf9b2170347d6336b80c022ee92b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv47"/><title type="x-s3">True Friendship.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv47"/> <div sID="gen14052" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> A friend loveth at all times, and a brother is born for adversity. <div eID="gen14052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14053" type="x-p"/> This intimates the strength of those bonds by which we are bound to each other and which we ought to be sensible of. 1. Friends must be constant to each other <hi type="italic">at all times.</hi> That is not true friendship which is not constant; it will be so if it be sincere, and actuated by a good principle. Those that are fanciful or selfish in their friendship will love no longer than their humour is pleased and their interest served, and therefore their affections turn with the wind and change with the weather. Swallow-friends, that fly to you in summer, but are gone in winter; such friends there is no loss of. But if the friendship be prudent, generous, and cordial, if I love my friend because he is wise, and virtuous, and good, as long as he continues so, though he fall into poverty and disgrace, still I shall love him. Christ is a friend that loves at all times (<reference osisRef="John.13.1">John xiii. 1</reference>) and we must so love him, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.35">Rom. viii. 35</reference>. 2. Relations must in a special manner be careful and tender of one another in affliction: <hi type="italic">A brother is born</hi> to succour a brother or sister in distress, to whom he is joined so closely by nature that he may the more sensibly feel from their burdens, and be the more strongly inclined and engaged, as it were by instinct, to help them. We must often consider what we were <hi type="italic">born for,</hi> not only as men, but as in such a station and relation. <hi type="italic">Who knows but we came</hi> into such a family <hi type="italic">for such a time as this?</hi> We do not answer the end of our relations if we do not do the duty of them. Some take it thus: <hi type="italic">A friend that loves at all times is born</hi> (that is, becomes) <hi type="italic">a brother in adversity,</hi> and is so to be valued.
entries.7200e4de3718a17672b0d959b8c2831d372567e4: <div eID="gen14053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14054" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> A man void of understanding striketh hands, <hi type="italic">and</hi> becometh surety in the presence of his friend. <div eID="gen14054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14055" type="x-p"/> Though Solomon had commended friendship in adversity (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">v. 17</reference>), yet let not any, under pretence of being generous to their friends, be unjust to their families and wrong them; one part of our duty must be made to consist with another. Note, 1. It is a piece of wisdom to keep out of debt as much as may be, especially to dread suretiship. There may be a just occasion for a man to pass his word for his friend in his absence, till he come to engage himself; but to be <hi type="italic">surety in the presence of his friend,</hi> when he is upon the spot, supposes that his own word will not be taken, he being deemed insolvent or dishonest, and then who can with safety pass his word for him? 2. Those that are <hi type="italic">void of understanding</hi> are commonly taken in this snare, to the prejudice of their families, and therefore ought not to be trusted too far with their own affairs, but to be under direction.
entries.356509f92d11482a5b5a834da4212f2a5d9ced4f: <div eID="gen14055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14056" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">19</hi> He loveth transgression that loveth strife: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that exalteth his gate seeketh destruction. <div eID="gen14056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14057" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Those that are quarrelsome involve themselves in a great deal of guilt: <hi type="italic">He that loves strife,</hi> that in his worldly business loves to go to law, in religion loves controversies, and in common conversation loves to thwart and fall out, that is never well but when he is in the fire, <hi type="italic">he loves transgression;</hi> for a great deal of sin attends that sin, and the way of it is down-hill. He pretends to stand up for truth, and for his honour and right, but really he loves sin, which God hates. 2. Those that are ambitious and aspiring expose themselves to a great deal of trouble, such as often ends in their ruin: <hi type="italic">He that exalts his gate,</hi> builds a stately house, at least a fine frontispiece, that he may overtop and outshine his neighbours, seeks his own destruction and takes a deal of pains to ruin himself; he makes his gate so large that his house and estate go out at it.  <div eID="gen14057" type="x-p"/>
entries.b2b309042065c673420ae82725b2c357ddfa938f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv48"/><title type="x-s3">Folly and Wickedness.</title> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv48"/> <div sID="gen14058" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">20</hi> He that hath a froward heart findeth no good: and he that hath a perverse tongue falleth into mischief. <div eID="gen14058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14059" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. Framing ill designs will be of no advantage to us; there is nothing got by them: <hi type="italic">He that has a froward heart,</hi> that sows discord and is full of resentment, cannot promise himself to get by it sufficient to counterbalance the loss of his repose and reputation, nor can he take any rational satisfaction in it; he <hi type="italic">finds no good.</hi> 2. Giving ill language will be a great disadvantage to us: <hi type="italic">He that has a perverse tongue,</hi> spiteful and abusive, scurrilous or backbiting, <hi type="italic">falls into</hi> one <hi type="italic">mischief</hi> or other, loses his friends, provokes his enemies, and pulls trouble upon his own head. Many a one has paid dearly for an unbridled tongue.
entries.43df5e7bd6334a16b1904f9657dc5fa01a27809d: <div eID="gen14059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14060" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> He that begetteth a fool <hi type="italic">doeth it</hi> to his sorrow: and the father of a fool hath no joy. <div eID="gen14060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14061" type="x-p"/> This expresses that very emphatically which many wise and good men feel very sensibly, what a grievous vexatious thing it is to have a foolish wicked child. See here, 1. How uncertain all our creature-comforts are, so that we are often not only disappointed in them, but that proves the greatest cross in which we promised ourselves most satisfaction. There was <hi type="italic">joy when a man-child was born into the world,</hi> and yet, if he prove vicious, his own father will wish he had never been born. The name of Absalom signifies his <hi type="italic">father's peace,</hi> but he was his greatest trouble. It should moderate the desire of having children, and the delights of their parents in them, that they may prove a grief to them; yet it should silence the murmurings of the afflicted father in that case that if his son be a fool he is a fool of his own begetting, and therefore he must make the best of him, and take it up as his cross, the rather because Adam begets a son in his own likeness. 2. How unwise we are in suffering one affliction (and that of an untoward child as likely as any other) to drown the sense of a thousand mercies: <hi type="italic">The father of a fool</hi> lays that so much to heart that he <hi type="italic">has no joy</hi> of any thing else. For this he may thank himself; there are joys sufficient to counterbalance even that sorrow.
entries.714cda37c9fd4d9c05f0792e6f9986a39ddcf79d: <div eID="gen14061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">22</hi> A merry heart doeth good <hi type="italic">like</hi> a medicine: but a broken spirit drieth the bones. <div eID="gen14062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. It is healthful to be cheerful. The Lord is for the body, and has provided for it, not only meat, but medicine, and has here told us that the best medicine is <hi type="italic">a merry heart,</hi> not a heart addicted to vain, carnal, sensual mirth; Solomon himself said of that mirth, It is not medicine, but madness; it is not food, but poison; <hi type="italic">what doth it?</hi> But he means a heart rejoicing in God, and serving him with gladness, and then taking the comfort of outward enjoyments and particularly that of pleasant conversation. It is a great mercy that God gives us leave to be cheerful and cause to be cheerful, especially if by his grace he gives us hearts to be cheerful. This <hi type="italic">does good to a medicine</hi> (so some read it); it will make physic more efficient. Or <hi type="italic">it does good as a medicine</hi> to the body, making it easy and fit for business. But, if mirth be a medicine (understand it of diversion and recreation), it must be used sparingly, only when there is occasion, not turned into food, and it must be used medicinally, <hi type="italic">sub regimine—as a prescribed regimen,</hi> and by rule. 2. The sorrows of the mind often contribute very much to the sickliness of the body: <hi type="italic">A broken spirit,</hi> sunk by the burden of afflictions, and especially a conscience wounded with the sense of guilt and fear of wrath, <hi type="italic">dries the bones,</hi> wastes the radical moisture, exhausts the very marrow, and makes the body a mere skeleton. We should therefore watch and pray against all melancholy dispositions, for they lead us into trouble as well as into temptation.
entries.c701bff88090024cec3bf47d355ba1f86cf0fc2c: <div eID="gen14063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14064" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">23</hi> A wicked <hi type="italic">man</hi> taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment. <div eID="gen14064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14065" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. What an evil thing bribery is: He is <hi type="italic">a wicked man</hi> that will <hi type="italic">take a gift</hi> to engage him to give a false testimony, verdict, or judgment; when he does it he is ashamed of it, for he takes it, with all the secresy imaginable, <hi type="italic">out of the bosom</hi> where he knows it is laid ready for him; it is industriously concealed, and so slyly that, if he could, he would hide it from his own conscience. <hi type="italic">A gift is taken out of the bosom of a wicked man</hi> (so some read it); for he is a bad man that gives bribes, as well as he that takes them. 2. What a powerful thing it is. It is of such force that it <hi type="italic">perverts the ways of judgment.</hi> The course of justice is not only obstructed, but turned into injustice; and the greatest wrongs are done under colour of doing right.
entries.5ede66b00ed074a5a41db11c6338c1c11c9e14e0: <div eID="gen14065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14066" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Wisdom <hi type="italic">is</hi> before him that hath understanding; but the eyes of a fool <hi type="italic">are</hi> in the ends of the earth. <div eID="gen14066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> Note, 1. He is to be reckoned an intelligent man that not only has wisdom, but has it ready when he has occasion for it. He lays his <hi type="italic">wisdom before him,</hi> as his card and compass which he steers by, has his eye always upon it, as he that writes has on his copy; and then he has it <hi type="italic">before him;</hi> it is not to seek, but still at hand. 2. He that has a giddy head, a roving rambling fancy, will never be fit for any solid business. He is a fool, and good for nothing, whose <hi type="italic">eyes are in the ends of the earth,</hi> here, and there and every where, any where but where they should be, who cannot fix his thoughts to one subject nor pursue any one purpose with any thing of steadiness. When his mind should be applied to his study and business it is filled with a thousand things foreign and impertinent.
entries.b1cee17f7782f0aa8c11ba9381208b115ba7e119: <div eID="gen14067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14068" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">25</hi> A foolish son <hi type="italic">is</hi> a grief to his father, and bitterness to her that bare him. <div eID="gen14068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14069" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. Wicked children are an affliction to both their parents. They are an occasion of <hi type="italic">anger</hi> to the father (so the word signifies), because they contemn his authority, but of sorrow and <hi type="italic">bitterness</hi> to the mother, because they abuse her tenderness. The parents, being joint-sufferers, should therefore bring mutual comfort to bear them up under it, and strive to make it as easy as they can, the mother to mollify the father's anger, the father to alleviate the mother's grief. 2. That Solomon often repeats this remark, probably because it was his own case; however, it is a common case.
entries.6e30cbd189c485f8c978cb2b93f8920b7ec2efa6: <div eID="gen14069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14070" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">26</hi> Also to punish the just <hi type="italic">is</hi> not good, <hi type="italic">nor</hi> to strike princes for equity. <div eID="gen14070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14071" type="x-p"/> In differences that happen between magistrates and subjects, and such differences often arise, 1. Let magistrates see to it that they never <hi type="italic">punish the just,</hi> that they be in no case a <hi type="italic">terror to good works,</hi> for that is to abuse their power and betray that great trust which is reposed in them. It is <hi type="italic">not good,</hi> that is, it is a very evil thing, and will end ill, whatever end they may aim at in it. When princes become tyrants and persecutors their thrones will be neither easy nor firm. 2. Let subjects see to it that they do not find fault with the government for doing its duty, for it is a wicked thing <hi type="italic">to strike princes for equity,</hi> by defaming their administration or by any secret attempts against them to strike at them, as the ten tribes that revolted reflected upon Solomon for imposing necessary taxes. Some read it, <hi type="italic">Nor to strike the ingenuous for equity.</hi> Magistrates must take heed that none suffer under them for well doing; nor must parents <hi type="italic">provoke their children to wrath</hi> by unjust rebukes.
entries.bd0b8830fc4509d8f877c980b25d5c5a6a015a20: <div eID="gen14071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14072" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> He that hath knowledge spareth his words: <hi type="italic">and</hi> a man of understanding is of an excellent spirit. <hi type="super">28</hi> Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: <hi type="italic">and</hi> he that shutteth his lips <hi type="italic">is esteemed</hi> a man of understanding. <div eID="gen14072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14073" type="x-p"/> Two ways a man may show himself to be a wise man:—1. By the good temper, the sweetness and the sedateness, of his mind: <hi type="italic">A man of understanding is of an excellent spirit,</hi> a <hi type="italic">precious spirit</hi> (so the word is); he is one that looks well to his spirit, that it be as it should be, and so keeps it in an even frame, easy to himself and pleasant to others. A gracious spirit is a precious spirit, and renders a man amiable and <hi type="italic">more excellent than his neighbour.</hi> He is of a <hi type="italic">cool spirit</hi> (so some read it), not heated with passion, nor put into any tumult or disorder by the <hi type="italic">impetus</hi> of any corrupt affection, but even and stayed. A cool head with a warm heart is an admirable composition. 2. By the good government of his tongue. (1.) A wise man will be <hi type="italic">of few words,</hi> as being afraid of speaking amiss: <hi type="italic">He that has knowledge,</hi> and aims to do good with it, is careful, when he does speak to speak to the purpose, and says little in order that he may take time to deliberate. He <hi type="italic">spares his words,</hi> because they are better spared than ill-spent. (2.) This is generally taken for such a sure indication of wisdom that a fool may gain the reputation of being a wise man if he have but wit enough to hold his tongue, to hear, and see, and say little. If a fool hold his peace, men of candour will think him wise, because nothing appears to the contrary, and because it will be thought that he is making observations on what others say, and gaining experience, and is consulting with himself what he shall say, that he may speak pertinently. See how easy it is to gain men's good opinion and to impose upon them. But when a <hi type="italic">fool holds his peace</hi> God knows his heart, and the folly that is bound up there; thoughts are words to him, and therefore he cannot be deceived in his judgment of men.  <chapter eID="Prov.17"/> <div eID="gen14073" type="x-p"/>

entries.a9721408a7f371e430e23dc4cbdba2c3764ba8cd: <div eID="gen24378" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen24379" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24380" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24380" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen24379" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen24381" type="x-p"/> Contentment. The wise servant. The Lord tries the heart. Children a crown to their parents. We should hide our neighbour's faults. The poor should not be despised. Litigations and quarrels to be avoided. Wealth is useless to a fool. The good friend. A fool may pass for a wise man when he holds his peace. <div eID="gen24381" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24382" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen24382" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24383" type="x-p"/> Better is a dry morsel - Peace and contentment, and especially domestic peace, are beyond all other blessings. <div eID="gen24383" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24384" type="x-p"/> A house full of sacrifices - A Hindoo priest, who officiates at a festival, sometimes receives so many offeringss that his house is filled with them, so that many of them are damaged before they can be used - Ward.
entries.4d22f2b4f32854ef0c8ca78d37b743b7afbfc567: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen24384" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24385" type="x-p"/> The fining pot is for silver - When silver is mixed, or suspected to be mixed, with base metal, it must be subjected to such a test as the cupel to purify it. And gold also must be purified by the action of the fire. So God tries hearts. He sends afflictions which penetrate the soul, and give a man to see his state, so that he may apply to the spirit of judgment and the spirit of burning, to destroy what cannot stand the fire, to separate and burn up all the dross.
entries.e9c3ebf67981f9cb2630f1d3375310702379dc34: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen24385" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24386" type="x-p"/> A wicked doer giveth heed - An evil heart is disposed and ever ready to receive evil; and liars delight in lies.
entries.84d9d1c70e4bbc618cecc52f263081c4dc9017c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen24386" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24387" type="x-p"/> He that is glad at calamity - He who is pleased to hear of the misfortune of another will, in the course of God's just government, have his own multiplied.
entries.3c0fd451ebf1ee2a55cc6ad0acc9ae8ece2392f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen24387" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24388" type="x-p"/> Excellent speech becometh not a fool - This proverb is suitable to those who affect, in public speaking, fine language, which neither comports with their ordinary conversation, nor with their education. Often fine words are injudiciously brought in, and are as unbecoming and irrelevant as a cart wheel among clockwork.
entries.190aafb58d6181837512bc2a67f9f64ec9798213: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen24388" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24389" type="x-p"/> A gift is as a precious stone - It both enriches and ornaments. In the latter clause there is an evident allusion to cut stones. Whithersoever you turn them, they reflect the light, are brilliant and beautiful.
entries.8caa1fa56ff83d53b390d91ff22bba2a1cb81444: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen24389" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24390" type="x-p"/> A reproof entereth more - Though the rod, judiciously applied, is a great instrument of knowledge, yet it is of no use where incurable dulness or want of intellect, prevails. Besides, there are generous dispositions on which counsel will work more than stripes.
entries.61d0ea085d60c88c0b11f3bc220de9ba0b37d1f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen24390" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24391" type="x-p"/> Let a bear robbed of her whelps - At which times such animals are peculiarly fierce. See the note on <reference osisRef="2Sam.17.8">2Sam 17:8</reference>.
entries.59cd4272575bd0104c5a461ee8c62815a9850e6c: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen24391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24392" type="x-p"/> Whoso rewardeth evil for good - Here is a most awful warning. As many persons are guilty of the sin of ingratitude, and of paying kindness with unkindness, and good with evil, it is no wonder we find so much wretchedness among men; for God's word cannot fail; evil shall not depart from the houses and families of such persons.
entries.e0bcfe5e0637575f6754de3ce9fa112075cf5bfa: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen24392" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24393" type="x-p"/> The beginning of strife is as when one letteth out water - As soon as the smallest breach is made in the dike or dam, the water begins to press from all parts towards the breach; the resistance becomes too great to be successfully opposed, so that dikes and all are speedily swept away. Such is the beginning of contentions, quarrels, lawsuits, etc. <div eID="gen24393" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24394" type="x-p"/> Leave off contention, before it be meddled with - As you see what an altercation must lead to, therefore do not begin it. Before it be mingled together, התגלע hithgalla, before the spirits of the contending parties come into conflict - are joined together in battle, and begin to deal out mutual reflections and reproaches. When you see that the dispute is likely to take this turn, leave it off immediately.
entries.b6996a35e97d2e470eda199b7ebbf673788fc9c8: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen24394" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> A friend loveth at all times - Equally in adversity as in prosperity. And a brother, according to the ties and interests of consanguinity, is born to support and comfort a brother in distress.
entries.aef1888853ae6f3ec01abb7b9b71be66a5c5402f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen24395" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24396" type="x-p"/> Striketh hands - Striking each other's hands, or shaking hands, was anciently the form in concluding a contract. See notes on <reference osisRef="Pro.6.1">Pro 6:1</reference>.
entries.e08022f1053f1c06693c39f0099c95426e502ff3: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen24396" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24397" type="x-p"/> He that exalteth his gate - In different parts of Palestine they are obliged to have the doors of their courts and houses very low, not more than three feet high, to prevent the Arabs, who scarcely ever leave the backs of their horses, from riding into the courts and houses, and spoiling their goods. He, then, who, through pride and ostentation, made a high gate, exposed himself to destruction; and is said here to seek it, because he must know that this would be a necessary consequence of exalting his gate. But although the above is a fact, yet possibly gate is here taken for the mouth; and the exalting of the gate may mean proud boasting and arrogant speaking, such as has a tendency to kindle and maintain strife. And this interpretation seems to agree better with the scope of the context than the above.
entries.b70760ba1857986801d1f747aaa8479f0093dc48: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen24397" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> A merry heart doeth good like a medicine - Instead of גהה gehah, a medicine, it appears that the Chaldee and Syriac had read in their copies גוה gevah, the body, as they translate in this way. This makes the apposition here more complete: "A merry heart doeth good to the body; but a broken spirit drieth the bones." Nothing has such a direct tendency to ruin health and waste out life as grief, anxiety, fretfulness, bad tempers, etc. All these work death.
entries.5a6fd1e2c83f3f11d068a38f73f81e7f4681392c: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen24398" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> A gift out of the bosom - Out of his purse; as in their bosoms, above their girdles, the Asiatics carry their purses. I have often observed this.
entries.71c2e263a682d119bbf07341f22ac6e07db556bc: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen24399" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24400" type="x-p"/> Are in the ends of the earth - Wisdom is within the sight and reach at every man: but he whose desires are scattered abroad, who is always aiming at impossible things, or is of an unsteady disposition, is not likely to find it.
entries.af6baf128bcd3589aef5bf9731212bbe729a6a3a: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen24400" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24401" type="x-p"/> Nor to strike princes for equity - To fall out with the ruler of the people, and to take off his head under pretense of his not being a just or equitable governor, is unjust. To kill a king on the ground of justice is a most dreadful omen to any land. Where was it ever done, that it promoted the public prosperity? No experiment of this kind has ever yet succeeded, howsoever worthless the king might be.
entries.82e2584fa83cb4401baa4012b6e2e2a87ec9f2a0: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen24401" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24402" type="x-p"/> Even a fool - He is counted wise as to that particular. He may know that he cannot speak well, and he has sense enough to keep from speaking. He is, as to that particular, a wise fool. <div eID="gen24402" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen24403" type="x-p"/> A man may be golden-mouthed and silver-tongued in eloquence; but to know when and where to speak and to be silent, is better than diamonds. But who that thinks he can speak well can refrain from speaking? His tongue has no rest.  <chapter eID="Prov.17"/> <div eID="gen24403" type="x-p"/>

entries.505238cfc1b9e9bb5c123c37764d4acc62608755: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.1">Pro 17:1</reference> <div eID="gen11250" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11251" type="x-p"/> A comparative proverb with טוב, pairing with <reference osisRef="Prov.16.32">Pro 16:32</reference> : <div eID="gen11251" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11252" type="x-p"/> Better a dry piece of bread, and quietness therewith, <div eID="gen11252" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11253" type="x-p"/> Than a house full of slain beasts with unquietness. <div eID="gen11253" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11254" type="x-p"/> Similar to this in form and contents are Pro 15:16. and Pro 16:8. פּת חרבה is a piece of bread (פת, fem., as <reference osisRef="Prov.23.8">Pro 23:8</reference>) without savoury drink (Theodotion, καθ ̓ ἑαυτόν, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, nothing with it), cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.7.10">Lev 7:10</reference>, a meat-offering without the pouring out of oil. זבחים are not sacrificial gifts (Hitzig), but, as always, slain animals, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, either offerings or banquets of slain beasts; it is the old name of the שׁלמים (cf. <reference osisRef="Exod.18.12">Exo 18:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.24.5">Exo 24:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14">Pro 7:14</reference>), part of which only were offered on the altar, and part presented as a banquet; and זבח (in contradist. to טבח, <reference osisRef="Lev.9.2">Lev 9:2</reference>; 43:16) denotes generally any kind of consecrated festival in connection with the worship of God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.29">1Sa 20:29</reference>; cf. Gen 31:54. “Festivals of hatred” are festivals with hatred. מלא is part. with object.-accus.; in general מלא forms a constructive, מלא occurs only once (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.11">Jer 6:11</reference>), and מלאי not at all. We have already, <reference osisRef="Prov.7.14">Pro 7:14</reference>, remarked on the degenerating of the shelamı̂m feasts; from this proverb it is to be concluded that the merriment and the excitement bordering on intoxication (cf. with Hitzig, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.13">1Sa 1:13</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.3">1Sa 1:3</reference>), such as frequently at the Kirmsen merry-makings, brought quarrels and strife, so that the poor who ate his dry bread in quiet peace could look on all this noise and tumult without envy.
entries.e4c2f4d0be73a2448e9fd22d767eb8d68790a146: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.2">Pro 17:2</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.2">2</reference> A prudent servant shall rule over the degenerate son;    And he divides the inheritance among the brethren. <div eID="gen11254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11255" type="x-p"/> Regarding the contrasts of משׂכּיל and מבישׁ, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.10.5">Pro 10:5</reference>; Pro 14:35. The printed editions present בּבן־מבישׁ in genit. connection: a son of the scandalous class, which is admissible; but Cod. 1294 and Cod. <hi type="italic">Jaman</hi>,<note placement="foot">The Cod. brought by Sapiir from Jemen, of which there is an account in the preface to the edition of <hi type="italic">Isaiah</hi> by Baer and me.</note> <div eID="gen11255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11256" type="x-p"/> Erf. No. 2, 3, write בּבן מבישׁ (with <hi type="italic">Tsere</hi> and <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>), and that is perhaps right, after <reference osisRef="Prov.10.5">Pro 10:5</reference>; Pro 17:25. The futures have here also a fut. signification: they say to what it will come. Grotius remarks, with reference to this: <hi type="italic">manumissus tutor filiis relinquetur</hi>; יחלק <hi type="italic">tutorio officio</hi>. But if he is a conscientious, unselfish tutor, he will not enrich himself by property which belongs to another; and thus, though not without provision, he is yet without an inheritance. And yet the supplanting of the degenerate is brought about by this, that he loses his inheritance, and the intelligent servant steps into his place. Has one then to suppose that the master of the house makes his servant a co-heir with his own children, and at the same time names him as his executor? That were a bad anachronism. The idea of the διαθήκη was, at the time when this proverb was coined, one unknown - Israelitish iniquity knows only the intestate right of inheritance, regulated by lineal and gradual succession. Then, if one thinks of the degenerate son, that he is disowned by the father, but that the intelligent servant is not rewarded during the life of his master for his true services, and that, after the death of the master, to such a degree he possesses the esteem and confidence of the family, that he it is who divides the inheritance among the brethren, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, occupies the place amongst them of distributor of the inheritance, not: takes a portion of the inheritance, for חלק has not the double meaning of the Lat. <hi type="italic">participare</hi>; it means to divide, and may, with בּ, mean “to give a part of anything” (<reference osisRef="Job.39.17">Job 39:17</reference>); but, with the accus., nothing else than to distribute, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Josh.18.2">Jos 18:2</reference>, where it is to be translated: “whose inheritance had not yet been distributed (not yet given to them).” Jerome, <hi type="italic">haereditatem dividet</hi>; and thus all translators, from the lxx to Luther.
entries.564da4010cac445cecdcac39ebc6f911a39ae926: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.3">Pro 17:3</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.3">3</reference> The fining-pot for silver, and the furnace for gold;    And a trier of hearts is Jahve. <div eID="gen11256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11257" type="x-p"/> An emblematical proverb, which means that Jahve is for the heart what the smelting-pot (from צרף, to change, particularly to melt, to refine) is for silver, and what the smelting furnace (כוּר, from כּוּר, R. כר, to round, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.20">Exo 22:20</reference>) is for gold, that Jahve is for the heart, viz., a trier (בחן, to grind, to try by grinding, here as at <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">Psa 7:10</reference>) of their nature and their contents, for which, of the proof of metals, is elsewhere (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.2">Pro 16:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.2">Pro 21:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.24.12">Pro 24:12</reference>) used the word (cf. בּחון, the essay-master, <reference osisRef="Jer.6.7">Jer 6:7</reference>) תּכן, weigher, or דּורשׁ, searcher (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.9">1Ch 28:9</reference>). Wherever the subject spoken of is God, the searcher of hearts, the plur. לבּות, once לבבות ecno ,, is used; the form לבבים occurs only in the <hi type="italic">status conjunctus</hi> with the suffix. In <reference osisRef="Prov.27.21">Pro 27:21</reference> there follow the two figures, with which there is formed a <hi type="italic">priamel</hi>, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.26.3">Pro 26:3</reference>, another <hi type="italic">tertium comparationis</hi>.
entries.f8b0f0ce9ce6c3710e986c65b979409b3fbe7149: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.4">Pro 17:4</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.4">4</reference> A profligate person giveth heed to perverse lips;    Falsehood listeneth to a destructive tongue. <div eID="gen11257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11258" type="x-p"/> The meaning, at all events, is, that whoever gives ear with delight to words which are morally reprobate, and aimed at the destruction of neighbours, thereby characterizes himself as a profligate. Though מרע is probably not pred. but subj., yet so that what follows does not describe the מרע (the profligate hearkens...), but stamps him who does this as a מרע (a profligate, or, as we say: only a profligate...). מרע, for מרע, is warranted by <reference osisRef="Isa.9.16">Isa 9:16</reference>, where מרע (not מרע ton, according to which the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. here translates ἀπὸ κακοῦ) is testified to not only by correct codd. and editions, but also by the Masora (cf. <hi type="italic">Michlol</hi> 116b). הקשׁיב (from קשׁב, R. קש, to stiffen, or, as we say, to prick, viz., the ear) is generally united with ל or אל, but, as here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">Pro 29:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.19">Jer 6:19</reference>, also with על. און, wickedness, is the absolute contrast of a pious and philanthropic mind; הוּת, from הוּה, not in the sense of eagerness, as <reference osisRef="Prov.10.3">Pro 10:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.6">Pro 11:6</reference>, but of yawning depth, abyss, catastrophe (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Ps.5.10">Psa 5:10</reference>), is equivalent to entire destruction - the two genitives denote the property of the lips and the tongue (<hi type="italic">labium nequam, lingua perniciosa</hi>), on the side of that which it instrumentally aims at (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.36.4">Psa 36:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.52.4">Psa 52:4</reference>): practising mischief, destructive plans. שׁקר beginning the second line is generally regarded as the subj. parallel with מרע, as Luther, after Jerome, “A wicked man gives heed to wicked mouths, and a false man listens willingly to scandalous tongues.” It is possible that שׁקר denotes incarnate falsehood, as רמיּה, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.27">Pro 12:27</reference>, incarnate slothfulness, cf. מרמה, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.25">Pro 14:25</reference>, and perhaps also <reference osisRef="Prov.12.17">Pro 12:17</reference>; צדק, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Psa 58:2</reference>, תּוּשׁיּה, Mic 6:9; יצר סמוּך, <reference osisRef="Isa.26.13">Isa 26:13</reference>, etc., where, without supplying אישׁ (אנשׁי), the property stands instead of the person possession that property. The clause, that falsehood listeneth to a deceitful tongue, means that he who listens to it characterizes himself thereby, according to the proverb, <hi type="italic">simile simili gaudet</hi>, as a liar. But only as a liar? The punctuation before us, which represents מרע by <hi type="italic">Dechi</hi> as subj., or also pred., takes שׁקר מזין as obj. with מזין as its governing word, and why should not that be the view intended? The representation of the obj. is an inversion less bold than <reference osisRef="Isa.22.2">Isa 22:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.22">Isa 8:22</reference>, and that על here should not be so closely connected with the verb of hearing, as 4a lies near by this, that הקשׁיב על is elsewhere found, but not האזין על. Jewish interpreters, taking שׁקר as obj., try some other meaning of מזין than <hi type="italic">auscultans</hi>; but neither זון, to approach, nor זין, to arm (<hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ψεῦδος ὁπλίζει), gives a meaning suitable to this place. מזין is equivalent to מאזין. As אאזין, <reference osisRef="Job.32.11">Job 32:11</reference>, is contracted into אזין, so must מאזין, if the character of the part. shall be preserved, become מזין, mediated by מיזין.
entries.1baf0e53a44093ed66657670405baa525096a5f2: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.5">Pro 17:5</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.5">5</reference> He that mocketh the poor reproacheth his Maker;    He that rejoiceth over calamity remains not unpunished. <div eID="gen11258" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11259" type="x-p"/> Line first is a variation of Pro 14:31. God is, according to <reference osisRef="Prov.22.2">Pro 22:2</reference>, the creator of the poor as well as of the rich. The poor, as a man, and as poor, is the work of God, the creator and governor of all things; thus, he who mocketh the poor, mocketh Him who called him into existence, and appointed him his lowly place. But in general, compassion and pity, and not joy (שׂמח ל, commonly with ל, of the person, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, Obad. Oba 1:12, the usual formula for ἐπιχαιρεκακία), is appropriate in the presence of misfortune (איד, from אוּד, to be heavily burdened), for such joy, even if he on whom the misfortune fell were our enemy, is a <hi type="italic">peccatum mortale</hi>, Job 31:29. There is indeed a hallowed joy at the actual revelation in history of the divine righteousness; but this would not be a hallowed joy if it were not united with deep sorrow over those who, accessible to no warning, have despised grace, and, by adding sin to sin, have provoked God’s anger.
entries.a949978fb377c2e5408306d1d9785a301011c4c2: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.6">Pro 17:6</reference> <div eID="gen11259" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11260" type="x-p"/> With this verse this series of proverbs closes as it began: <div eID="gen11260" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11261" type="x-p"/> A diadem of the old are children’s children, <div eID="gen11261" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11262" type="x-p"/> And the glory of children are their parents. <div eID="gen11262" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11263" type="x-p"/> Children are a blessing from God (Ps 127-128); ); thus, a family circle consisting of children and grandchildren (including great-grandchildren) is as a crown of glory surrounding the grey-haired patriarch; and again, children have glory and honour in their parents, for to have a man of an honoured name, or of a blessed memory, as a father, is the most effective commendation, and has for the son, even though he is unlike his father, always important and beneficial consequences. In 6b a fact of experience is expressed, from which has proceeded the rank of inherited nobility recognised among men - one may abnegate his social rights, but yet he himself is and remains a part of the moral order of the world. The lxx has a distich after <reference osisRef="Prov.17.4">Pro 17:4</reference> the Vatican text places it after <reference osisRef="Prov.17.6">Pro 17:6</reference> : “The whole world of wealth belongs to the faithful, but to the unfaithful not even an <hi type="italic">obolus</hi>.” Lagarde supposes that ὄλος ὁ κόσμος τῶν χρημάτων is a translation of שׁפעת יתר, instead of שׂפת יתר, 7a. But this ingenious conjecture does not amount to the regarding of this distich as a variation of Pro 17:7. <div eID="gen11263" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11264" type="x-p"/> The proverbs following, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.7-Prov.17.10">Pro 17:7-10</reference>, appear to be united acrostically by the succession of the letters ש (שׂ, שׁ) and ת.
entries.40670d22e2923b7f7182505dbeab938b27a5ee35: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.7">Pro 17:7</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.7">7</reference> It does not become a fool to speak loftily,    How much less do lying lips a noble! <div eID="gen11264" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11265" type="x-p"/> As at Isa 32:5., נבל and נדיב are placed opposite to one another; the latter is the nobly magnanimous man, the former the man who thinks foolishly and acts profligately, whom it does not become to use lofty words, who thereby makes the impression of his vulgarity so much the more repulsive (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.2.10">Job 2:10</reference>). שּׂפת יתר (not יתר, for the word belongs to those which retain their <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi> or <hi type="italic">Segol</hi>, <hi type="italic">in pausa</hi>) is neither elevated (soaring) (Ewald) nor diffuse (Jo. Ernst Jungius in Oetinger: <hi type="italic">lingua dicax ac sermonem ultra quam decorum verbis extendere solita</hi>), rather imperative (Bertheau), better presumptuous (Hitzig) words, properly words of superfluity, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, of superabundant self-consciousness and high pretension (cf. the transitive bearing of the Arab. watr with ὑβρίζειν, from ὑπέρ, Aryan upar, <hi type="italic">Job</hi>, p. 363). Rightly Meîri, שׂפת נאוה ושׂררה. It produces a disagreeable impression, when a man of vulgar mind and of rude conduct, instead of keeping himself in retirement, makes himself of importance, and weighty in a shameless, impudent manner (cf. Ps. 12:9, where זלּוּת, <hi type="italic">vilitas</hi>, in a moral sense); but yet more repulsive is the contrast, when a man in whom one is justified in expecting nobility of mind, in accordance with his life-position and calling, degrades himself by uttering deceitful words. Regarding the אף כּי, concluding <hi type="italic">a minori ad majus</hi>, we have already spoken at <reference osisRef="Prov.11.31">Pro 11:31</reference>; Pro 15:11. R. Ismael, in <hi type="italic">Bereschith Rabba</hi>, at 44:8, reckons ten such conclusions <hi type="italic">a minori ad majus</hi> in the Scriptures, but there are just as many <hi type="italic">quanto magis</hi>. The right accentuation (<hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, in Cod. 1294) is here אף כי־לנדיב, transformed from אף כי־לנדיב, according to <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>, xviii. 2.
entries.fa523692d8ea849b2ae395f7533836335eec8f60: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">Pro 17:8</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.8">8</reference> The gift of bribery appears a jewel to its receiver;    Whitherso'er he turneth himself he acteth prudently. <div eID="gen11265" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11266" type="x-p"/> How 8b is to be understood is shown by <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.47">1Sa 14:47</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.1.7">Jos 1:7</reference>; the <hi type="italic">quoque se vertit, prudenter rem agit</hi>, has accordingly in both sentences the person meant by בּעליו as subject, not the gift (Hitzig), of which ישׂכּיל, “it maketh prosperous,” is not said, for השׂכּיל means, used only of persons, prudent, and therefore successful, fortunate conduct. Such is said of him who has to give (Luther): he presses through with it whithersoever he turns. But the making of בּעיני the subj. does not accord with this: this means gift to one who has to give, appears to open doors and hearts, not merely as a golden key, it is truly such to him. Thus בעליו, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.3.27">Pro 3:27</reference>, will be meant of him to whom the present is brought, or to whom a claim thereto is given. But שׂחד means here not the gift of seasonable liberality (Zöckler), but, as always, the gift of bribery, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, a gift by which one seeks to purchase for himself (<reference osisRef="Prov.17.23">Pro 17:23</reference>) preference on the part of a judge, or to mitigate the displeasure of a high lord (<reference osisRef="Prov.21.14">Pro 21:14</reference>); here (for one does not let it depend merely on the faithfulness of another to his duty) it is that by which one seeks to secure an advantage to himself. The proverb expresses a fact of experience. The gift of bribery, to which, as to a well-known approved means, השּׂחד, refers, appears to him who receives and accepts it (Targ.) as a stone of pleasantness, a charming, precious stone, a jewel (<hi type="italic">Juwêl</hi> from <hi type="italic">joie</hi> = <hi type="italic">gaudium</hi>); it determines and impels him to apply all his understanding, in order that he may reach the goal for which it shall be his reward. What he at first regarded as difficult, yea, impossible, that he now prudently carries out, and brings to a successful conclusion, wherever he turns himself, overcoming the seemingly insurmountable hindrances; for the enticement of the gift lifts him, as with a charm, above himself, for covetousness is a characteristic feature of human nature - <hi type="italic">pecuniae obediunt omnia</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.19">Ecc 10:19</reference>, Vulg.).
entries.4629d59fefa9193925181da6df5a091022f53d22: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.9">Pro 17:9</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.9">9</reference> He covereth transgressions who seeketh after love,    And he who always brings back a matter separateth friends. <div eID="gen11266" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11267" type="x-p"/> The pred. stands first in the simple clause with the order of the words not inverted. That מכסה פשׁע is also to be interpreted here as pred. (cf. 19a) is shown by <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pro 10:12</reference>, according to which love covereth all transgressions. We write מכסּה־פּשׂע with <hi type="italic">Dag. forte conjunctivum</hi> of פ (as of ב in <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.6">Eze 18:6</reference>), and <hi type="italic">Gaja</hi> with the <hi type="italic">Sheva</hi>, according to the <hi type="italic">Meth.-Setzung</hi>, §37; the punctuation מכסּה פּשׁע also occurs. What the expression “to seek love” here means, is to be judged, with Hitzig, after Zep 2:3; 1Co 14:1. It is in no case equivalent to seek to gain the love of another, rather to seek to preserve the love of men towards one another, but it is to be understood not after 9b, but after <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Pro 10:12</reference> : he seeks to prove love who does not strike on the great bell when his neighbour has sinned however grievously against him, does not in a scandal-loving manner make much ado about it, and takes care not thereby to widen the breach between men who stand near to one another, but endeavours by a reconciling, soothing, rectifying influence, to mitigate the evil, instead of making it worse. He, on the contrary, who repeats the matter (שׁנה with ב of the obj., to come back with something, as <reference osisRef="Prov.26.11">Pro 26:11</reference>), <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, turns always back again to the unpleasant occurrence (Theodotion, δευτερῶν ἐν λόγῳ; Symmachus, δευτερῶν λόγον, as Sir. 7:14; 19:7), divides friends (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.16.28">Pro 16:28</reference>), for he purposely fosters the strife, the disharmony, ill-will, and estrangement which the offence produced; while the noble man, who has love for his motive and his aim, by prudent silence contributes to bring the offence and the division which it occasioned into forgetfulness.
entries.5debe65ce695c22d7849ae4cde328076bf13cce4: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.10">Pro 17:10</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.10">10</reference> One reproof maketh more impression on a wise man      Than if one reckoned a hundred to the fool <div eID="gen11267" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11268" type="x-p"/> One of the few proverbs which begin with a future, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 12:26. It expresses what influence there is in one reproof with a wise man (מבין, <reference osisRef="Prov.8.9">Pro 8:9</reference>); גּערה is the reproof expressed by the post-bibl. נזיפה .lbib, as the lowest grade of disciplinary punishment, <hi type="italic">admonitio</hi>, connected with warning. The verbal form תהת is the reading of the lxx and Syr. (συντρίβει ἀπειλὴ καρδίαν φρονίμου) for they read תחת גערה לב מבין, derived from חתת, and thus תּחת (from <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. החת); thus Luther: reproof alarms more the intelligent, but חחת with ב of the obj. is not Hebr.; on the contrary, the reading of the lxx is in accordance with the usage of the language, and, besides, is suitable. It is, however, first to be seen whether the traditional text stands in need of this correction. As <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. תּחת, apart from the ult. accent. to be expected, gives no meaning. Also if one derives it from חתה, to snatch away, to take away, it gives no appropriate thought; besides, חתה is construed with the object. accus., and the <hi type="italic">fut. Apoc</hi>., in itself strange here, must be pointed either תּהת or תּחתּ (after יחדּ) (Böttcher, <hi type="italic">Lehrb</hi>. ii. p. 413). Thus יחת, as at <reference osisRef="Job.21.13">Job 21:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.21.13">Jer 21:13</reference>, will be <hi type="italic">fut</hi>. <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> of נחת = ינחת, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.3">Psa 38:3</reference> (Theodotion, Targ., Kimchi). With this derivation, also, תּחת is to be expected; the reference in the <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi> to Gesen. <hi type="italic">Lehrgebäude</hi>, §51, 1, Anm. 1, where, in an extremely inadequate way, the retrogression of the tone (נסוג אחור) is spoken of, is altogether inappropriate to this place; and Böttcher’s explanation of the ult. tone from an intended expressiveness is ungrammatical; but why should not תּחת, from נחת, with its first syllable originating from contraction, and thus having the tone be <hi type="italic">Milel</hi> as well as <hi type="italic">Milra</hi>, especially here, where it stands at the head of the sentence? With ב connected with it, נחת means: to descend into anything, to penetrate; Hitzig appropriately compares <hi type="italic">altius in pectus descendit</hi> of Sallust, <hi type="italic">Jug</hi>. 11. Jerome rightly, according to the sense: <hi type="italic">plus proficit</hi>, and the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἀνεῖ (read ὀνεῖ) ἀπειλὴ τῷ συνίοντι. In 10b מכּה (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.25.3">Deu 25:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.24">2Co 11:24</reference>) is to be supplied to מאה, not פאמים (an hundred times, which may be denoted correctly by מאה as well as מאת, <reference osisRef="Eccl.8.12">Ecc 8:12</reference>). With the wise (says a Talmudic proverb) a sign does as much as with the fool a stick does. Zehner, in his <hi type="italic">Adagia sacra</hi> (1601), cites Curtius (vii. 4): <hi type="italic">Nobilis equus umbra quoque virgae regitur, ignavus ne calcari quidem concitari potest</hi>.
entries.dee08c7fc3c0502d71c288f179e15ea9e33c226e: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.11">Pro 17:11</reference> <div eID="gen11268" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11269" type="x-p"/> Five proverbs of dangerous men against whom one has to be on his guard: 11 The rebellious seeketh only after evil,      And a cruel messenger is sent out against him. <div eID="gen11269" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11270" type="x-p"/> It is a question what is subj. and what obj. in 11a. It lies nearest to look on מרי as subj., and this word (from מרה, <hi type="italic">stringere</hi>, to make oneself exacting against any, to oppose, ἀντιτείνειν) is appropriate thereto; it occurs also at <reference osisRef="Ezek.2.7">Eze 2:7</reference> as <hi type="italic">abstr. pro concreto</hi>. That it is truly subj. appears from this, that בּקּשׁ רע, to seek after evil (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.29.10">Pro 29:10</reference>; 1Ki 20:7, etc.), is a connection of idea much more natural than בּקּשׁ מרי to seek after rebellion. Thus אך will be logically connected with רע, and the reading אך מרי will be preferred to the reading אך־מרי; אך (corresponding to the Arab. âinnama) belongs to those particles which are placed before the clause, without referring to the immediately following part of the sentence, for they are much more regarded as affecting the whole sentence (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <reference osisRef="Prov.13.10">Pro 13:10</reference>): the rebellious strives after nothing but only evil. Thus, as neut. obj. רע is rendered by the Syr., Targ., <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., and Luther; on the contrary, the older Greek translators and Jerome regard רע as the personal subject. If now, in reference to rebellion, the discourse is of a מלאך אכזרי, we are not, with Hitzig, to think of the demon of wild passions unfettered in the person of the rebellious, for that is a style of thought and of expression that is modern, not biblical; but the old unpoetic yet simply true remark remains: <hi type="italic">Loquendi formula inde petita quod regis aut summi magistratus minister rebelli supplicium nunciat infligitque</hi>. מלאך is <hi type="italic">n. officii</hi>, not <hi type="italic">naturae</hi>. Man as a messenger, and the spiritual being as messenger, are both called מלאך. Therefore one may not understand מלאך אכזרי, with the lxx, Jerome, and Luther, directly and exclusively of an angel of punishment. If one thinks of Jahve as the Person against whom the rebellion is made, then the idea of a heavenly messenger lies near, according to Psa 35:5., <reference osisRef="Ps.78.49">Psa 78:49</reference>; but the proverb is so meant, that it is not the less true if an earthly king sends out against a rebellious multitude a messenger with an unlimited commission, or an officer against a single man dangerous to the state, with strict directions to arrest him at all hazards. אכזרי we had already at <reference osisRef="Prov.12.10">Pro 12:10</reference>; the root קש חש means, to be dry, hard, without feeling. The fut. does not denote what may be done (Bertheau, Zöckler), which is contrary to the parallelism, the order of the words, and the style of the proverb, but what is done. And the relation of the clause is not, as Ewald interprets it, “scarcely does the sedition seek out evil when an inexorable messenger is sent.” Although this explanation is held by Ewald as “unimprovable,” yet it is incorrect, because אך in this sense demands, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.27.3">Gen 27:3</reference>, the perf. (strengthened by the <hi type="italic">infin. intensivus</hi>). The relation of the clause is, also, not such as Böttcher has interpreted it: a wicked man tries only scorn though a stern messenger is sent against him, but not because such a messenger is called אכזרי, against whom this “trying of scorn” helps nothing, so that it is not worth being spoken of; besides, שׁלּח or משׁלּח would have been used if this relation had been intended. We have in 11a and 11b, as also <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, at <reference osisRef="Prov.26.24">Pro 26:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.1">Pro 28:1</reference>, two clauses standing in internal reciprocal relation, but syntactically simply co-ordinated; the force lies in this, that a messenger who recognises no mitigating circumstances, and offers no pardon, is sent out against such an one.
