entries.5f32470c965ab846009c6b0f9c9428a685eb01d6: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.12">Pro 17:12</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.12">12</reference> Meet a bear robbed of one of her whelps,      Only not a fool in his folly. <div eID="gen11270" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11271" type="x-p"/> The name of the bear, as that of the cow, <reference osisRef="Job.21.10">Job 21:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.144.14">Psa 144:14</reference>, preserves its masculine form, even when used in reference to sexual relationship (Ewald, §174b); the <hi type="italic">ursa catulis orbata</hi> is proverbially a raging beast. How the abstract expression of the action פּגושׁ [to meet], here as <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.17.5">Psa 17:5</reference>, with the subj. following, must sound as finite (<hi type="italic">occurrat</hi>, may always meet), follows from ואל = ואל־יפגּשׁ (<hi type="italic">non autem occurrat</hi>). פּגושׁ has on the last syllable <hi type="italic">Mehuppach</hi>, and <hi type="italic">Zinnorith</hi> on the preceding open syllable (according to the rule, <hi type="italic">Accentssystem</hi>, vi. §5d).<note placement="foot">In the <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 18, the word is irregularly represented as <hi type="italic">Milel</hi> - a closed syllable with <hi type="italic">Cholem</hi> can suffer no retrogression of the tone.</note> שׁכּוּל, in the state of his folly, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, when he is in a paroxysm of his anger, corresponds with the conditional noun-adjective שׁכּוּל, for folly morbidly heightened is madness (cf. Hos 11:7; <hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 291f.).
entries.59275b71f627cbfae1ef033148ab48836d20dc09: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.13">Pro 17:13</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.13">13</reference> He that returneth evil for good,      From his house evil shall not depart. <div eID="gen11271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11272" type="x-p"/> If ingratitude appertains to the sinful manifestations of ignoble selfishness, how much more sinful still is black ingratitude, which recompenses evil for good! (משׁיב, as <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.21">1Sa 25:21</reference>, syn. גּמל, to requite, <reference osisRef="Prov.3.30">Pro 3:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.31.12">Pro 31:12</reference>; שׁלּם, to reimburse, <reference osisRef="Prov.20.22">Pro 20:22</reference>). Instead of תמישׁ, the Kerı̂ reads תמוּשׁ; but that this verb, with a middle vowel, may be 'י'ע as well as 'ו'ע, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.2">Psa 55:2</reference> shows.
entries.6a9efe568b23f99481e92943ac16e197f5993cd7: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.14">Pro 17:14</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.14">14</reference> As one letteth out water is the beginning of a strife;      But cease thou from such strife ere it comes to showing teeth. <div eID="gen11272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11273" type="x-p"/> The meaning of this verb פּטר is certain: it means to break forth; and transitively, like Arab. faṭr, to bring forth from a cleft, to make to break forth, to let go free (Theodotion, ἀπολύων; Jerome, <hi type="italic">dimittit</hi>; <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. ἀφιείς). The lxx, since it translates by ἐξουσίαν δίδωσι, thinks on the juristic signification, which occurs in the Chronicles: to make free, or to declare so; but here פּוטר מים (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding the <hi type="italic">Metheg</hi> at <reference osisRef="Prov.14.31">Pro 14:31</reference>) is, as Luther translates, one who tears away the dam from the waters. And ראשׁית מדון is not accus. dependent on פוטר, to be supplied (Hitzig: he unfetters water who the beginning of strife, viz., unfetters); but the part. is used as at <reference osisRef="Prov.10.17">Pro 10:17</reference> : one who unfetters the water is the beginning of strife, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, he is thus related to it as when one... This is an addition to the free use of the part. in the language of the Mishna, where one would expect the <hi type="italic">infin</hi>., <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, בּזורע (= בּזרע), if one sows, בּמזיד (= בּזדון), of wantonness. It is thus unnecessary, with Ewald, to interpret פוטר as neut., which lets water go = a water-outbreak; פוטר is meant personally; it represents one who breaks through a water-dam, withdraws the restraint of the water, opens a sluice, and then emblematically the proverb says: thus conditioned is the beginning of a strife. Then follows the warning to let go such strife (הריב, with the article used in the more elevated style, not without emphasis), to break from it, to separate it from oneself ere it reach a dangerous height. This is expressed by לפני התגּלּע, a verb occurring only here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.18.1">Pro 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.3">Pro 20:3</reference>, always in the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. The Targum (misunderstood by Gesenius after Buxtorf; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., to the contrary, Levy, under the word צדי II) translates it at <reference osisRef="Prov.18.1">Pro 18:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.20.3">Pro 20:3</reference>, as the Syr., by “to mock,” also Aquila, who has at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.3">Pro 20:3</reference>, ἐξυβρισθήσεται, and the lxx at <reference osisRef="Prov.18.1">Pro 18:1</reference>, ἐπονείδιστος ἔσται, and Jerome, who has this in all the three passages, render the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. in this sense, passively. In this passage before us, the Targ., as Hitzig gives it, translates, “before it heats itself,” but that is an error occasioned by Buxtorf; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the contrary, Levy, under the word קריא (κύριος); this translation, however, has a representative in Haja Gaon, who appeals for גלע, to glow, to <hi type="italic">Nidda</hi> viii. 2.<note placement="foot">Vid., Simon Nascher's<hi type="italic">Der Gaon Haja u. seine giest. Thätig.</hi> p. 15.</note> <div eID="gen11273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11274" type="x-p"/> Elsewhere the lxx, at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.3">Pro 20:3</reference>, συμπλέκεται (where Jerome, with the amalgamation of the two significations, <hi type="italic">miscentur contumeliis</hi>); Kimchi and others gloss it by התערב, and, according to this, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. translates, πρὸ τοῦ συνχυθῆναι (τὴν ἔριν); Luther, “before thou art mingled therein.” But all these explanations of the word: <hi type="italic">insultare, excandescere</hi>, and <hi type="italic">commisceri</hi>, are etymologically inadmissible. Bertheau’s and Zöckler’s “roll itself forth” is connected at least with a meaning rightly belonging to the R. גל. But the Arab. shows, that not the meaning <hi type="italic">volvere</hi>, but that of <hi type="italic">retegere</hi> is to be adopted. Aruch<note placement="foot"><hi type="italic">Vid</hi>., p. 109, note.</note> for <hi type="italic">Nidda</hi> viii. 2 refers to the Arab., where a wound is designated as יכולה להגּלע ולהוציא דם, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, as breaking up, as it were, when the crust of that which is nearly healed is broken off (Maimuni glosses the word by להתקלף, were uncrusted), and blood again comes forth. The meaning <hi type="italic">retegere</hi> requires here, however, another distinction. The explanation mentioned there by Aruch: before the strife becomes public to thee, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, approaches thee, is not sufficient. The verbal stem גלע is the stronger power of גלה, and means laying bare; but here, not as there, in the Mishna of a wound covered with a crust. The Arab. jal' means to quarrel with another, properly to show him the teeth, the <hi type="italic">Poël</hi> or the tendency-stem from jali'a, to have the mouth standing open, so that one shows his teeth; and the Syr. glaṣ, with its offshoots and derivatives, has also this meaning of <hi type="italic">ringi</hi>, opening the mouth to show, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to make bare the teeth. Schultens has established this explanation of the words, and Gesenius further establishes it in the Thesaurus, according to which Fleischer also remarks, “גלע, of showing the teeth, the exposing of the teeth by the wide opening of the mouth, as happens in bitter quarrels.” But הריב does not agree with this. Hitzig’s translation, “before the strife shows its teeth,” is as modern as in <reference osisRef="Prov.17.11">Pro 17:11</reference> is the passion of the unfettered demon, and Fleischer’s <hi type="italic">prius vero quam exacerbetur rixa</hi> renders the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. in a sense unnecessarily generalized for <reference osisRef="Prov.18.1">Pro 18:1</reference> and Pro 20:3. The accentuation, which separates להתגלע from הריב by <hi type="italic">Rebia</hi> <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi>, is correct. One may translate, as Schultens, <hi type="italic">antequam dentes stringantur</hi>, or, since the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. has sometimes a reciprocal signification, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Gen.42.1">Gen 42:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.41.8">Psa 41:8</reference> : ere one reciprocally shows his teeth, Hitzig unjustly takes exception to the inversion הריב נטושׁ. Why should not the object precede, as at Hos 12:1-14 :15, the נטוש, placed with emphasis at the end? The same inversion for a like reason occurs at Ecc 5:6.
entries.7e3303dca5674d591a5c1adae8ee2d933e433703: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.15">Pro 17:15</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.15">15</reference> He that acquitteth the guilty and condemneth the righteous -      An abomination to Jahve are they both. <div eID="gen11274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11275" type="x-p"/> The proverb is against the partisan judge who is open to bribery, like <reference osisRef="Prov.24.24">Pro 24:24</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference>, where, with reference to such, the announcement of punishment is emphatically made. רשׁע and צדּיק, in a forensic sense, are equivalent to <hi type="italic">sons</hi> (<hi type="italic">reus</hi>) and <hi type="italic">insons</hi>. גּם (cf. the Arab. jmy'na, altogether, but particularly the Pers. ham and the Turkish <hi type="italic">dkhy</hi> standing wholly thus in the numeral) is here, as at <reference osisRef="Gen.27.45">Gen 27:45</reference>, equivalent to יחדּיו, <reference osisRef="Jer.46.12">Jer 46:12</reference> (in its unions = united). Whoever pronounces sentence of justification on the guilty, appears as if he must be judged more mildly than he who condemns the guiltless, but both the one and the other alike are an abhorrence to God. <div eID="gen11275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11276" type="x-p"/> We take <reference osisRef="Prov.17.16-Prov.17.21">Pro 17:16-21</reference> together. This group beings with a proverb of the heartless, and ends with one of the perverse-hearted; and between these there are not wanting noticeable points of contact between the proverbs that follow one another.
entries.eccdd3d195b1cfe256a7d393a6009367c86c1192: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.16">Pro 17:16</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.16">16</reference> Why the ready money in the hand of the fool;      To get wisdom when he has yet no heart? <div eID="gen11276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11277" type="x-p"/> The question is made pointed by זה, thus not: why the ready money when...? Is it to obtain wisdom? - the whole is but one question, the reason of which is founded in לבו אין (thus to be accented with <hi type="italic">Mugrash</hi> going before).<note placement="foot">If we write ולב־ with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, then we have to accentuate לקנות חכמה with <hi type="italic">Tarcha</hi> <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>, because the <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi> word in this writing has not two syllables before the tone. This sequence of accents if found in the Codd. Ven. 1521, 1615, Basel 1619, while most editions have לקנות חכמה ולב־אין, which is false. But according to MSS we have ולב without <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>, and that is right according to the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi> rules of the metrical <hi type="italic">Accentuationssystem</hi>; <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., <hi type="italic">Torath Emeth</hi>, p. 40.</note> <div eID="gen11277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11278" type="x-p"/> The fool, perhaps, even makes some endeavours, for he goes to the school of the wise, to follow out their admonitions, קנה חכמה (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.5">Pro 4:5</reference>, etc.), and it costs him something (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.7">Pro 4:7</reference>), but all to no purpose, for he has no heart. By this it is not meant that knowledge, for which he pays his honorarium, remains, it may be, in his head, but goes not to his heart, and thus becomes an unfruitful theory; but the heart is equivalent to the understanding, in the sense in which the heart appears as the previous condition to the attainment of wisdom (<reference osisRef="Prov.18.15">Pro 18:15</reference>), and as something to be gained before all (<reference osisRef="Prov.15.32">Pro 15:32</reference>), viz., understanding, as the fitting intellectual and practical <hi type="italic">habitus</hi> to the reception, the appropriation, and realization of wisdom, the ability rightly to comprehend the fulness of the communicated knowledge, and to adopt it as an independent possession, that which the Greek called νοῦς, as in that “golden proverb” of Democrates: πολλοὶ πολυμαθέες νοῦν οὐκ ἔχουσι, or as in <reference osisRef="Luke.24.25">Luk 24:25</reference>, where it is said that the Lord opened τὸν νοῦν of His disciples to understand the Scriptures. In the lxx a distich follows <reference osisRef="Prov.17.16">Pro 17:16</reference>, which is made up of 19b and 20b, and contains a varied translation of these two lines.
entries.e7dc80ba06e77dfc76f295569d3c2a0bf623fc61: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">Pro 17:17</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.17">17</reference> At all times the right friend shows himself loving;      And as a brother is he born for adversity. <div eID="gen11278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11279" type="x-p"/> Brother is more than friend, he stands to one nearer than a friend does, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.14">Psa 35:14</reference>; but the relation of a friend may deepen itself into a spiritual, moral brotherhood, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.24">Psa 18:24</reference>, and there is no name of friend that sounds dearer than אחי, 2Sa 1:26. 17a and 17b are, according to this, related to each other climactically. The friend meant in 17a is a true friend. Of no other is it said that he loves בּכל־עת, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, makes his love manifest; and also the article in הרע not only here gives to the word more body, but stamps it as an ideal-word: the friend who corresponds to the idea of such an one.<note placement="foot">The Arab. grammarians say that the article in this case stands, l'astfrâgh khsânas âljnas, as an exhaustive expression of all essential properties of the genus, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, to express the full ideal realization of the idea in that which is named.</note> <div eID="gen11279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11280" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. of the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>., in the sense “to associate” (Ewald), cannot therefore be הרע, because רע is not derived from רעע, but from רעה. Thus there exists no contrast between 17a and 17b, so that the love of a friend is thought of, in contradistinction to that of a brother, as without permanency (Fl.); but 17b means that the true friend shows himself in the time of need, and that thus the friendship becomes closer, like that between brothers. The statements do not refer to two kinds of friends; this is seen from the circumstance that אח has not the article, as הרע has. It is not the subj. but pred., as אדם, <reference osisRef="Job.11.12">Job 11:12</reference> : sooner is a wild ass born or born again as a man. The meaning of הוּלד there, as at Psa 87:5., borders on the notion of <hi type="italic">regenerari</hi>; here the idea is not essentially much less, for by the saying that the friend is born in the time of need, as a brother, is meant that he then for the first time shows himself as a friend, he receives the right status or baptism of such an one, and is, as it were, born into personal brotherly relationship to the sorely-tried friend. The translation <hi type="italic">comprobatur</hi> (Jerome) and <hi type="italic">erfunden</hi> [is found out] (Luther) obliterates the peculiar and thus intentional expression, for נולד is not at all a metaphor used for passing into the light - the two passages in Proverbs and in Job have not their parallel. לצרה is not equivalent to בּצרה (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>), for the interchange of the prep. in 17a and 17b would then be without any apparent reason. But Hitzig’s translation also: as a brother he is born of adversity, is impossible, for ל after נודל and ילּד always designates that for which the birth is an advantage, not that from which it proceeds. Thus ל will be that of the purpose: for the purpose of the need, - not indeed to suffer (<reference osisRef="Job.5.7">Job 5:7</reference>) on account of it, but to bear it in sympathy, and to help to bear it. Rightly Fleischer: <hi type="italic">frater autem ad aerumnam</hi> (<hi type="italic">sc</hi>. <hi type="italic">levandam et removendam</hi>) <hi type="italic">nascitur</hi>. The lxx gives this sense to the ל: ἀδελφοὶ δὲ ἐν ἀνάγκαις χρήσιμοι ἔστωσαν, τοῦτο γὰρ χάριν γεννῶνται.
entries.9b5a73ee89f5ea8ae6d00369b0303feaadba8a7f: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.18">Pro 17:18</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.18">18</reference> A man void of understanding is he who striketh hands,      Who becometh surety with his neighbour. <div eID="gen11280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11281" type="x-p"/> Cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1-Prov.6.5">Pro 6:1-5</reference>, where the warning against suretyship is given at large, and the reasons for it are adduced. It is incorrect to translate (Gesen., Hitzig, and others) לפני רעהוּ, with the lxx, Jerome, the Syr., Targ., and Luther, “for his neighbour;” to become surety for any one is ערב ל, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.1">Pro 6:1</reference>, or, with the object. accus. <reference osisRef="Prov.11.15">Pro 11:15</reference>, another suitable prep. is בּעד; but לפני never means <hi type="italic">pro</hi> (ὑπέρ), for at <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.16">1Sa 1:16</reference> it means “to the person,” and <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.31">2Sa 3:31</reference>, “before Abner’s corpse (bier).” רעהוּ is thus here the person with whom the suretyship is entered into; he can be called the רע of him who gives bail, so much the more as the reception of the bail supposes that both are well known to each other. Here also Fleischer rightly translates: <hi type="italic">apud alterum</hi> (<hi type="italic">sc</hi>. <hi type="italic">creditorem pro debitore</hi>).
entries.fabca43451ea7ca76bb7bf5da154092344c2c52d: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.19">Pro 17:19</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.19">19</reference> He loveth sin who loveth strife;      He who maketh high his doors seeketh destruction. <div eID="gen11281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11282" type="x-p"/> A synthetic distich. Böttcher finds the reason of the pairing of these two lines in the relationship between a mouth and a door (cf. Mic 7:6, פּתחי פיך). Hitzig goes further, and supposes that 19b figuratively expresses what boastfulness brings upon itself. Against Geier, Schultens, and others, who understand פּתחו directly of the mouth, he rightly remarks that הגדּיל פה is not heard of, and that הגדּיל פה taht dn would be used instead. But the two lines harmonize, without this interchangeable reference of <hi type="italic">os</hi> and <hi type="italic">ostium</hi>. <hi type="italic">Zanksucht</hi> [quarrelsomeness] and <hi type="italic">Prunksucht</hi> [ostentation] are related as the symptoms of selfishness. But both bear their sentence in themselves. He who has pleasure in quarrelling has pleasure in evil, for he commits himself to the way of great sinning, and draws others along with him; and he who cannot have the door of his house high enough and splendid enough, prepares thereby for himself, against his will, the destruction of his house. An old Hebrew proverb says, כל העוסק בבנין יתמסכן, <hi type="italic">aedificandi nimis studiosus ad mendicitatem redigitur</hi>. Both parts of this verse refer to one and the same individual, for the <hi type="italic">insanum aedificandi studium</hi> goes only too often hand in hand with unjust and heartless litigation.
entries.868ba691607a8fd43342b0ce2a8f542cc7d3e65a: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.20">Pro 17:20</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.20">20</reference> He that is of a false heart findeth no good;      And he that goeth astray with his tongue falleth into evil. <div eID="gen11282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11283" type="x-p"/> Regarding עקּשׁ־לב, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 11:20. In the parallel member, נהפּך בּלשׁונו is he who twists or winds (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., at <reference osisRef="Prov.2.12">Pro 2:12</reference>) with his tongue, going about concealing and falsifying the truth. The phrase ונהפּך (the connecting form before a word with a prep.) is syntactically possible, but the Masora designates the word, in contradistinction to ונהפּך, pointed with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, <reference osisRef="Lev.13.16">Lev 13:16</reference>, with לית as <hi type="italic">unicum</hi>, thus requires ונהפּך, as is also found in Codd. The contrast of רעה is here טוב, also neut., as <reference osisRef="Prov.13.21">Pro 13:21</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.16.20">Pro 16:20</reference>, and רע, Pro 13:17.
entries.0e4f614467b8037fb8f09becb92eb47f6233c820: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.21">Pro 17:21</reference> <div eID="gen11283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11284" type="x-p"/> The first three parts of the old Solomonic Book of Proverbs ((1) <reference osisRef="Prov.10.12">Prov 10-12</reference>; (<reference osisRef="Prov.10.2">2</reference>) <reference osisRef="Prov.13.1-Prov.13.15">13:1-15</reference>:<reference osisRef="Prov.13.19">19</reference>; (<reference osisRef="Prov.13.3">3</reference>) <reference osisRef="Prov.15.20-Prov.15.17">15:20-17</reference>:<reference osisRef="Prov.15.20">20</reference>) are now followed by the fourth part. We recognise it as striking the same keynote as Pro 10:1. In <reference osisRef="Prov.17.21">Pro 17:21</reference> it resounds once more, here commencing a part; there, <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference>, beginning the second group of proverbs. The first closes, as it begins, with a proverb of the fool. 21 He that begetteth a fool, it is to his sorrow;      And the father of a fool hath no joy. <div eID="gen11284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11285" type="x-p"/> It is admissible to supply ילדו, developing itself from ילד, before לתוּגה לו (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., regarding this passive formation, at <reference osisRef="Prov.10.1">Pro 10:1</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.14.13">Pro 14:13</reference>), as at <reference osisRef="Isa.66.3">Isa 66:3</reference>, מעלה (Fl.: <hi type="italic">in maerorem sibi genuit h. e. ideo videtur genuisse ut sibi maerorem crearet</hi>); but not less admissible is it to interpret לתוגה לו as a noun-clause corresponding to the ולא־ישׂמח (thus to be written with <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>): it brings grief to him. According as one understands this as an expectation, or as a consequence, ילד, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.23.24">Pro 23:24</reference>, is rendered either <hi type="italic">qui gignit</hi> or <hi type="italic">qui genuit</hi>. With נבל, seldom occurring in the Book of Proverbs (only here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.17.7">Pro 17:7</reference>), כּסיל, occurring not unfrequently, is interchanged. Schultens rightly defines the latter etymologically: <hi type="italic">marcidus h. e. qui ad virtutem, pietatem, vigorem omnem vitae spiritualis medullitus emarcuit</hi>; and the former: <hi type="italic">elumbis et mollitie segnitieve fractus</hi>, the intellectually heavy and sluggish (cf. Arab. kasal, laziness; kaslân, the lazy).<note placement="foot">Nöldeke’s assertion (Art. <hi type="italic">Orion</hi> in Schenkel’s <hi type="italic">Bibel-Lexicon</hi>) that the Arab. <hi type="italic">kasal</hi> corresponds to the Hebr. כּשׁל proceeds from the twofold supposition, that the meaning to be lazy underlies the meaning to totter (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., also Dietrich in Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Heb. Wörterbuch</hi>), and that the Hebr. ס must correspond with the Arab. š. The former supposition is untenable, the latter is far removed (cf. <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, כּסּא and kursı̂, ספר and sifr, מסכּן and miskı̂n). The verb כּשׁל, Aram. תּקל, is unknown in the Arab.</note>
entries.3a5daf2f75efd544e1a2a9ee14c5befbbb34699a: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.22">Pro 17:22</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.22">22</reference> A joyful heart bringeth good recovery;      And a broken spirit drieth the bones. <div eID="gen11285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11286" type="x-p"/> The heart is the centre of the individual life, and the condition and the tone of the heart communicates itself to this life, even to its outermost circumference; the spirit is the power of self-consciousness which, according as it is lifted up or broken, also lifts up or breaks down the condition of the body (<hi type="italic">Psychol</hi>. p. 199), <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., the similar contrasted phrases לב שׂמח and רוּח נכאה, Pro 15:13. The ἄπ. λεγ. גּהה (here and there in Codd. incorrectly written גּיהה) has nothing to do with the Arab. jihat, which does not mean sight, but direction, and is formed from wjah (whence wajah, sight), like עדה, congregation, from ועד (יעד). The Syr., Targ. (perhaps also Symmachus: ἀγαθύνει ἡλικίαν; Jerome: <hi type="italic">aetatem floridam facit</hi>; Luther: makes the life <hi type="italic">lüstig</hi> [cheerful]) translate it by body; but for this גּוה (גּויּה) is used, and that is a word of an entirely different root from גּהה. To what verb this refers is shown by Hos 5:13 : ולא־יגהה מכּם מזור, and healed not for you her ulcerous wound. מזור is the compress, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, the bandage closing up the ulcer, then also the ulcer-wound itself; and גּהה is the contrary of עלה, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jer 8:22</reference>; it means the removing of the bandage and the healing of the wound. This is confirmed by the Syr. gho, which in like manner is construed with min, and means to be delivered from something (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Bernstein’s <hi type="italic">Lex. Syr.</hi> to Kirsch’s <hi type="italic">Chrestomathie</hi>). The Aethiop. quadriliteral gâhgěh, to hinder, to cause to cease, corresponds to the causative Syr. agahish. Accordingly גּהה means to be in the condition of abatement, mitigation, healing; and גּהה (as synonym of כּהה, <reference osisRef="Neh.3.19">Neh 3:19</reference>, with which Parchon combines it), <hi type="italic">levamen, levatio</hi>, in the sense of bodily healing (lxx εὐεκτεῖν ποιεῖ; <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>., after Kimchi, ἀγαθυνεῖ θεραπείαν); and היטיב גּהה (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.15.2">Pro 15:2</reference>) denotes, to bring good improvement, to advance powerfully the recovery. Schultens compares the Arab. jahy, <hi type="italic">nitescere, disserenari</hi>, as Menahem has done ננהּ, but this word is one of the few words which are explained exclusively from the Syriac (and Aethiop.). גּרם (here and at <reference osisRef="Prov.25.15">Pro 25:15</reference>) is the word interchanging with עצם, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.30">Pro 15:30</reference>; Pro 16:24.
entries.7e7184d476eaa92b4d6bf69d9f930f504e1c6231: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.23">Pro 17:23</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.23">23</reference> Bribery from the bosom the godless receiveth,      To pervert the ways of justice. <div eID="gen11286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11287" type="x-p"/> Regarding שׂחד, <hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Pro 17:8. The idea of this word, as well as the clause containing the purpose, demand for the רשׁע a high judicial or administrative post. The bosom, חק (חיק), is, as <reference osisRef="Prov.16.23">Pro 16:23</reference>, that of the clothing. From the bosom, מחק, where it was kept concealed, the gift is brought forth, and is given into the bosom, בּחק, <reference osisRef="Prov.21.14">Pro 21:14</reference>, of him whose favour is to be obtained - an event taking place under four eyes, which purposely withdraws itself from the observation of any third person. Since this is done to give to the course of justice a direction contrary to rectitude, the giver of the bribe has not right on his side; and, under the circumstances, the favourable decision which he purchases may be at once the unrighteous sentence of a צדיק, accusing him, or accused by him, Pro 18:5.
entries.001dcb046ab57cad200c102385d0caab124deccd: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.24">Pro 17:24</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.24">24</reference> The understanding has his attention toward wisdom;      But the eyes of a fool are on the end of the earth. <div eID="gen11287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11288" type="x-p"/> Many interpreters explain, as Euchel: “The understanding finds wisdom everywhere; <div eID="gen11288" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11289" type="x-p"/> The eyes of the fool seek it at the end of the world.” <div eID="gen11289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11290" type="x-p"/> Ewald refers to <reference osisRef="Deut.30.11-Deut.30.14">Deu 30:11-14</reference> as an unfolding of the same thought. But although it may be said of the fool (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., on the contrary, <reference osisRef="Prov.15.14">Pro 15:14</reference>) that he seeks wisdom, only not at the right place, as at <reference osisRef="Prov.14.6">Pro 14:6</reference>, of the mocker that he seeks wisdom but in vain, yet here the order of the words, as well as the expression, lead us to another thought: before the eyes of the understanding את־פּניע, as <reference osisRef="Gen.33.18">Gen 33:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.11">1Sa 2:11</reference>, and frequently in the phrase 'את־פני ה, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.22">1Sa 1:22</reference>) wisdom lies as his aim, his object, the end after which he strives; on the contrary, the eyes of the fool, without keeping that one necessary thing in view, wander <hi type="italic">in alia omnia</hi>, and roam about what is far off, without having any fixed object. The fool is everywhere with his thoughts, except where he ought to be. Leaving out of view that which lies nearest, he loses himself in <hi type="italic">aliena</hi>. The understanding has an ever present theme of wisdom, which arrests his attention, and on which he concentrates himself; but the fool flutters about fantastically from one thing to another, and that which is to him precisely of least importance interests him the most.
entries.74d9c59bbc486b6d93b19f6cc3d333baaee2d661: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.25">Pro 17:25</reference> <div eID="gen11290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11291" type="x-p"/> The series of proverbs, v. 25-18:2, begins and closes in the same way as the preceding, and only <reference osisRef="Prov.17.26">Pro 17:26</reference> stands by itself without apparent connection. <div eID="gen11291" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11292" type="x-p"/> This verse begins connecting itself with <reference osisRef="Prov.17.21">Pro 17:21</reference> : <div eID="gen11292" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11293" type="x-p"/> A grief to his father is a foolish son, <div eID="gen11293" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11294" type="x-p"/> And a bitter woe for her that bare him. <div eID="gen11294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11295" type="x-p"/> The ἅπ. λεγ. ממר is formed from מרר (to be bitter, properly harsh), as מכס from כּסס. The Syr. and Targ. change the subst. into participles; some codd. also have ממר (after the forms מחל, מסב, מפר, מרע), but as may be expected in 25a, מבעיס. The dat. obj. instead of the accus. may be possible; the verse immediately following furnishes a sufficient example of this.
entries.f8d726a82d87fd73ac7cb7ffa00f244b08ec6b78: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.26">Pro 17:26</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.26">26</reference> Also to inflict punishment on the righteous is not good;      This, that one overthrows the noble on account of his rectitude. <div eID="gen11295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11296" type="x-p"/> Does the גּם [also] refer to a connection from which the proverb is separated? or is it tacitly supposed that there are many kinds of worthless men in the world, and that one from among them is brought forward? or is it meant, that to lay upon the righteous a pecuniary punishment is also not good? None of all these. The proverb must have a meaning complete in itself; and if pecuniary punishment and corporeal punishment were regarded as opposed to one another, 26b would then have begun with אף כּי (<hi type="italic">quanto magis percutere ingenuos</hi>). Here it is with גם as at <reference osisRef="Prov.20.11">Pro 20:11</reference>, and as with אך at 11a, and רק at <reference osisRef="Prov.13.10">Pro 13:10</reference> : according to the sense, it belongs not to the word next following, but to לצּדּיק; and ענשׁ (whence <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. ענושׁ, as <reference osisRef="Prov.21.11">Pro 21:11</reference>, with the ǎ in ע, cf. also עבד, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.10">Pro 11:10</reference>, for אבד) means here not specially to inflict a pecuniary fine, but generally to punish, for, as in mulctare, the meaning is generalized, elsewhere with the accus., <reference osisRef="Deut.22.19">Deu 22:19</reference>, here to give to any one to undergo punishment. The ruler is the servant of God, who has to preserve rectitude, εἰς ὀργὴν τῷ τὸ κακὸν πράσσοντι (<reference osisRef="Rom.13.14">Rom 13:14</reference>). It is not good when he makes his power to punish to be felt by the innocent as well as by the guilty. <div eID="gen11296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11297" type="x-p"/> In 26b, instead of הכּות, the proverb is continued with להכּות; לא־טוב, which is to be supplied, takes the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. alone when it precedes, and the <hi type="italic">inf</hi>. with ל when it follows, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.5">Pro 18:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.28.21">Pro 28:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.9">Pro 21:9</reference> (but cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.21.19">Pro 21:19</reference>). הכּות is the usual word for punishment by scourging, <reference osisRef="Deut.25.1-Deut.25.3">Deu 25:1-3</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.24">2Co 11:24</reference>, N.T. μαστιγοῦν, δίρειν, Rabb. מכּות, strokes, or מלקוּת from לקה, <hi type="italic">vapulare</hi>, to receive stripes. נדיבים are here those noble in disposition. The idea of נדיב fluctuates between <hi type="italic">generosus</hi> in an outward and in a moral sense, wherefore על־ישׁר, or rather עלי־ישׁר, is added; for the old editions, correct MSS, and <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, also Soncin. 1488, present עלי (<hi type="italic">vid</hi>., Norzi). Hitzig incorrectly explains this, “against what is due” (ישׁר, as <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Pro 11:24</reference>); also <reference osisRef="Ps.94.20">Psa 94:20</reference>, עלי־חק does not mean κατὰ προστάγματος (Symmachus), but ἐπὶ προστάγματι (lxx and Theod.), on the ground of right = <hi type="italic">praetextu juris</hi> (Vatabl.). Thus עלי־ישׁר means here neither against nor beyond what is due, but: on the ground of honourable conduct, making this (of course mistakenly) a lawful title to punishment; Aquila, ἐπὶ εὐθύτητι, cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.5.10">Mat 5:10</reference>, ἕνεκεν δικαιοσύνης. Besides, for על after הכּה, the causal signification lies nearest Num 22:32, cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.1.5">Isa 1:5</reference> (על־מה, on account of anything). If the power of punishment is abused to the punishing of the righteous, yea, even to the corporeal chastisement of the noble, and their straight, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, conscientious, firm, open conduct, is made a crime against them, that is not good - it is perversion of the idea of justice, and an iniquity which challenges the penal rectitude of the Most High (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Ecc 5:7</reference> [8]).
entries.a2278925d5d084efc5da5cb7c642a35b56be8437: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.27">Pro 17:27</reference> <reference osisRef="Prov.17.27">27</reference> He that keepeth his words to himself hath knowledge,      And the cool of temper is a man of understanding. <div eID="gen11297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11298" type="x-p"/> The first line here is a variation of Pro 10:19. The phrase ידע דּעת (here and at <reference osisRef="Dan.1.4">Dan 1:4</reference>) means to possess knowledge (<hi type="italic">novisse</hi>); more frequently it is בּינה ידע, <hi type="italic">e.g.</hi>, <reference osisRef="Prov.4.1">Pro 4:1</reference>, where ידע has the inchoative sense of <hi type="italic">noscere</hi>. In 27b the Kerı̂ is יקר־רוח. Jerome translates it <hi type="italic">pretiosi spiritus</hi>, the <hi type="italic">Venet</hi>. τίμιος τὸ πνεῦμα. Rashi glosses יקר here, as at <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.1">1Sa 3:1</reference>, by מנוע (thus to be read after codd.), <hi type="italic">retentus spiritu</hi>; most interpreters remark that the spirit here comes into view as expressing itself in words. It is scarcely correct to say that יקר דּברים could designate one who is sparing in his words, but יקר־רוּח is, according to the fundamental conception of the verb יקר, <hi type="italic">gravis spiritu</hi> (Schultens), of a dignified, composed spirit; it is a quiet seriousness proceeding from high conscientiousness, and maintaining itself in self-control, which is designated by this word. But the Chethı̂b וקר־רוּח presents almost the same description of character. קר from קרר (of the same root as יקר) means to be firm, unmoveable, καρτερὸν εἶναι, hence to be congealed, frozen, cold (cf. <hi type="italic">frigus</hi> with <hi type="italic">rigere</hi>, <hi type="italic">rigor</hi>), figuratively to be cold-blooded, passionless, quiet, composed (Fl.); cf. post-bibl. קרת רוּח (Arab. ḳurrat‛ain), cooling = refreshing, ἀνάψυξις (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.20">Act 3:20</reference>).<note placement="foot">“He has made my eye glowing” (askhn, cf. שׁחין) is in Arab. equivalent to “he has deeply troubled me.” The eye of the benevolent is bârid, and in the Semitic manner of expression, with deep psychological significance, it is said that the tears of sorrow are hot, but those of joy cold.</note> <div eID="gen11298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11299" type="x-p"/> Whether we read יקר or קר, in any case we are not to translate <hi type="italic">rarus spiritu</hi>, which, apart from the impossibility of the expression, makes 27b almost a tautological repetition of the thought of 27a. The first line recommends bridling of the tongue, in contrast to inconsiderate and untimely talk; the second line recommends coldness, <hi type="italic">i.e.</hi>, equanimity of spirit, in contrast to passionate heat.
entries.b1df78339488b81f7bc47408e4be00d8131396bc: <reference osisRef="Prov.17.28">Pro 17:28</reference> <div eID="gen11299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11300" type="x-p"/> Ver. 28 continues the same theme, the value of silence: <div eID="gen11300" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11301" type="x-p"/> Even a fool, when he keeps silence, is counted wise; <div eID="gen11301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11302" type="x-p"/> When he shutteth his mouth, discreet. <div eID="gen11302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11303" type="x-p"/> The subj. as well as the pred. of the first line avail for the second. אטם, <hi type="italic">obturare, occludere</hi>, usually of the closing the ear, is here transferred to the mouth. The <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. החרישׁ means <hi type="italic">mutum agere</hi> (cf. Arab. khrs, <hi type="italic">mutum esse</hi>), from חרשׁ, which, like κωφός, passes from the meaning <hi type="italic">surdus</hi> to that of <hi type="italic">mutus</hi> (Fl.). The words of <reference osisRef="Job.13.5">Job 13:5</reference>, and also those of Alexander: <hi type="italic">si tacuisses sapiens mansisses</hi>, are applicable to fools. An Arab. proverb says, “silence is the covering of the stupid.” In the epigrammatical hexameter, πᾶς τις ἀπαίδευτος φρονιμώτατός ἐστι σιωπῶν, the word σιωπῶν has the very same syntactical position as these two participles.<note placement="foot">Cf. C. Schultze’s <hi type="italic">Die bibl. Sprichwörter</hi> (1860), p. 60f.</note>  <chapter eID="Prov.17"/> <div eID="gen11303" type="x-p"/>
